reference: Runnable cases compare the builtin with the system GNU coreutils who on the same deterministic, private Linux utmp files. The Bash printf fixture encoder writes the Linux glibc 384-byte utmp record layout (fixed fields, record types and a UTC timestamp) independently of the candidate output. The metadata case uses Bash type/help builtins and a literal expected result. Additional fixtures encode little-endian integers and fixed-width fields directly from the Linux glibc 384-byte utmp ABI, with no candidate struct serialization or live records.
coverage: Builtin registration and availability of Bash help metadata.
Empty explicit utmp input, headers, ordinary rows, and -u formatting.
GNU who quick-count output with multiple user rows, a non-user row, and a partial trailing record.
Record type selection with -b, -d, -r, -a and composed -bd.
The -- end-of-options marker for a relative dash-leading fixture path.
Additional GNU field boundaries, selection combinations, aliases, and private input errors.
exclusions: Reading the live default /var/run/utmp database is deferred because representative live sessions require a disposable VM or injected fixture path.
No records are created, changed, or deleted in an account database.
Real terminal idle time, terminal permissions, and positive -m matches remain deferred; only unknown/nonmatching terminal states are qualified.
GNU two-word default-database invocation and optional DNS lookup features are outside the private-file scope.
Binary fixture encoding targets the Linux little-endian glibc 384-byte utmp ABI used by this runtime; other utmp ABIs need a separate independent encoder before reuse.

cases.purpose: Confirm Bash resolves who as a builtin and exposes its help metadata without reading a utmp file.
cases.script:
[[ $(type -t who) == builtin ]]
help_text=$(help who)
[[ -n $help_text ]]
printf 'who builtin help available\n'

cases.purpose: An explicitly named empty utmp file has no login records and produces no output.
Print headings alongside one valid USER_PROCESS record using -H.
Count two user records in -q mode, ignore a BOOT_TIME record under the default filter, and ignore a truncated trailing record.
Compare normal row formatting and -u output for a fixed UTC login timestamp, user, line, host, and pid.
Exercise -b, -d, -r, composed -bd, and -a against one fixture containing BOOT_TIME, DEAD_PROCESS, RUN_LVL, INIT_PROCESS, LOGIN_PROCESS, and USER_PROCESS records.
cases.script:
zpad() { local n=$1 i; for ((i=0;i<n;i++)); do printf '\000'; done; }
le() { local v=$1 n=$2 i b; for ((i=0;i<n;i++)); do printf -v b '\\%03o' "$(( (v >> (8*i)) & 255 ))"; printf '%b' "$b"; done; }
field() { printf '%s' "$1"; zpad "$(( $2 - ${#1} ))"; }
record() {
 le "$1" 2; zpad 2; le "${6:-1234}" 4
 field "$3" 32; field "${5:-}" 4; field "$2" 32; field "$4" 256
 le "${7:-0}" 2; le "${8:-0}" 2; zpad 4
 le 946684800 4; zpad 40
}
record 7 alice tty1 node-a > types.utmp
record 2 '' 'system boot' '' >> types.utmp
record 8 charlie tty3 '' >> types.utmp
record 1 runlevel 'run-level 5' '' >> types.utmp
record 6 login tty4 '' >> types.utmp
record 5 init tty5 '' >> types.utmp
who -b types.utmp
who -d types.utmp
who -r types.utmp
who -bd types.utmp
who -a types.utmp

cases.purpose: Compare read failure behavior on a private directory, without any system path.
Reject an unsupported flag before opening any database.
cases.script:
if who --not-a-who-option private.utmp; then exit 41; else rc=$?; fi
printf 'status=%s\n' "$rc"
